extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and publishers preparing scholarly books and articles using Chicago Notes & Bibliography style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and arranging notes, endnotes, and bibliographies (Chicago Notes & Bibliography system) for scholarly books and articles, including citation forms, bibliography structure, and name-entry conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Footnotes keyed to line numbers (use with verse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Footnotes keyed to line numbers—a device best used with verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With prose, the notes cannot be numbered until the text has been typeset. See 14.53.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endnotes keyed to page numbers with key phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Endnotes keyed to page numbers, with key phrases in bold and italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though unnumbered in the text, notes that share the same page have been numbered in the endnotes to facilitate reference to individual notes. See 14.53, 14.157.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing reprinted works (different title)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an article or chapter is reprinted under a different title, indicate the original publication and state 'Reprinted by permission.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Originally published as “Manet in His Generation: The Face of Painting in the 1860s,” Critical Inquiry 19, no. 1 (1992): 22-69, © 1992 by The University of Chicago. All rights reserved. Reprinted by permission.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing revised reprints
rubrics_metrics.description: If an article or chapter has been revised, indicate original publication in slightly different form and mention permission of author/publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Originally published in a slightly different form in The Metropolis in Modern Life, ed. Robert Moore Fisher (New York: Doubleday, 1955), 125-48. Reprinted by permission of the author and the publisher.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing public-domain/reprinted-from works
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work is in the public domain (such as government publications), indicate 'Reprinted from...' with full source details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Reprinted from Ambler Thompson and Barry N. Taylor, Guide for the Use of the International System of Units (SI) (Gaithersburg, MD: National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2008), 38-39.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Biographical notes placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief biographical note on author(s) may appear as an unnumbered note on the first page of each article/chapter or at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These identifying notes are unnecessary when the work includes a list of contributors with affiliations. Some electronic formats that do not support unnumbered footnotes may put biographical notes at the end of the article or chapter. See 1.64, 1.66.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special acknowledgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Special acknowledgments may be given in an unnumbered note, sometimes appended to the biographical information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include short acknowledgments of assistance or permissions; they are often unnumbered and placed with biographical notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding overlong notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Lengthy, discursive notes—especially footnotes—should be reduced or integrated into the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endnotes can accommodate lengthier commentary but should be limited judiciously. Complicated tabular material, lists, and other non-text entities should be put in an appendix. Example parenthetical: 'For a list of institutions involved, see appendix A.' See 14.44, 14.45, 1.59.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grouping several citations in one note
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce the number of note references by grouping several citations in a single note.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations are separated by semicolons and must appear in the same order as the text material they document. Take care to avoid ambiguity about what is being documented. See example text and corresponding single grouped note.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitting or including authors' given names in notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors’ given names may be omitted in a note when they appear in the text; include as needed for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inclusion of names in endnotes versus footnotes, see 14.48. In the provided example, authors’ given names are omitted in the note because they appear in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing sources in text to reduce notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite sources parenthetically in the text rather than in notes to reduce number of notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This works well for a string of consecutive citations that refer to the same source (with or without the use of ibid.). See 13.64-72 for discussion and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for frequently cited works
rubrics_metrics.description: If necessary, a frequently mentioned work may be cited by an abbreviation in text or subsequent notes, with the full citation provided at first mention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More helpful with footnotes than endnotes. Example: provide full citation once and thereafter cite as '(PI, 360)' if defined as 'hereafter cited in text as PI'. See 14.29-36, 14.60.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of abbreviations when many used
rubrics_metrics.description: When many abbreviations (say, ten or more) are used, list them alphabetically in a separate section titled 'Abbreviations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a book, the list may appear in front matter if footnotes are used or in the end matter preceding the endnotes if these are used. Include this list in the table of contents. Titles italicized in notes should be italicized in their abbreviated forms as well. See fig. 14.7 and 14.60.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of bibliographies to notes
rubrics_metrics.description: A full bibliography that includes all sources cited in the text supplies an overview of sources and indicates the scope of an author's research; it can serve as a key to shortened notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not all annotated works require a bibliography (full details can go in notes), an alphabetical bibliography is helpful and reader-friendly. See 14.61.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography format and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: A bibliography is most commonly a single alphabetical list by authors' last names and is normally placed at the end, preceding the index.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All sources—books, articles, dissertations—are alphabetically arranged. In multiauthor books or textbooks, each chapter may be followed by a brief bibliography. See 14.62, 14.65-71.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dividing a bibliography into sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide a bibliography into sections only if it makes the reader's job significantly easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate when including manuscript/archival sources, distinguishing different kinds of works (e.g., works by the writer vs. about the writer), or when the bibliography is a guide to further reading. When divisions are necessary, include a headnote and explanatory subheads; do not list a source in more than one section. See 14.63.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of bibliographies (categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select from bibliographic categories—full bibliography, selected bibliography, annotated bibliography, bibliographic essay, list of works by one author—based on purpose and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each kind has recommended heading and structure: 'Bibliography' or 'Works Cited' for full; 'Selected Bibliography' if not exhaustive (headnote explaining selection); 'Suggested Readings' for short lists; annotated entries may follow publication details or be indented; bibliographic essays are discursive and need not be alphabetized. See 14.64 and figures 14.8–14.11.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full bibliography definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A full bibliography includes all works cited, whether in text or in notes, excluding personal communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The usual heading is Bibliography, though Works Cited or Literature Cited may be used if no additional works are included. Some particularly relevant works consulted but not cited may also be listed. See 14.64.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selected bibliography guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author does not list all works cited, the title must indicate selection—e.g., 'Selected Bibliography'—and a headnote should explain principles of selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the list is short, titles like 'Suggested Readings' or 'Further Readings' may be used. See fig. 14.9 and 14.64.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotated bibliography formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotated bibliographies may place annotations after publication details (sometimes in brackets) or on a new indented line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotations provide readers with brief descriptions and are often more convenient than a bibliographic essay. See fig. 14.10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliographic essay usage
rubrics_metrics.description: A bibliographic essay treats the literature discursively and is less formal than an annotated bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works in the essay need not be alphabetized; subject divisions may be used freely. If a bibliography also exists, the essay should come first. If no bibliography exists, the essay must include full publication facts. See fig. 14.11.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of works by one author
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of works by a single author is usually arranged chronologically under headings like 'Published Works' or 'Writings [of Author].'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If several titles are listed for each year, dates may appear as subheads. See 14.64.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetizing: letter-by-letter vs word-by-word
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letter-by-letter alphabetizing (Chicago recommends) though the word-by-word system is accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under letter-by-letter, 'Fernandez, Angelines' precedes 'Fernan Gomez, Fernando'; word processors may produce word-by-word sorts and will require manual correction. Also adjust entries beginning with a 3-em dash as needed. See 14.66.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entries with more than one author: ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: A single-author entry precedes a multiauthor entry beginning with the same name; only the first author's name is inverted in the bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For successive entries with the same first author but different coauthors, alphabetize according to the coauthors' last names regardless of number of coauthors. See examples in 14.66.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the 3-em dash in bibliographies (general caveats)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 3-em dash (to replace a repeated name) is aimed primarily at publishers and editors; authors usually should not use it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: 3-em dashes do not work in computerized sorts, may obscure details like 'ed.' or 'trans.', and make it impractical to present an entry outside context. Publishers may decide not to use 3-em dashes; where not used, simply repeat authors' names. See 14.67.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-em dash for successive entries by same author
rubrics_metrics.description: For successive entries by the same author/editor/translator, a 3-em dash (followed by punctuation) replaces the name after the first appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alphabetization is by title of work. Abbreviations such as ed. or trans. must always be included and do not influence order. See 14.69–14.71.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-em dash for repeated multiple-author combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The 3-em dash can stand for the same two or more authors provided they are listed in the same order and no author appears for one source but not for the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations for editor, translator, etc., cannot be replaced by the 3-em dash and must always be listed explicitly. See 14.69.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-em dash for institutional/corporate authors
rubrics_metrics.description: The 3-em dash may be used for institutional or corporate authors to replace a repeated institutional name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that identical titles must be repeated. See 14.70.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetical order for titles by the same author
rubrics_metrics.description: In a bibliography (as opposed to a reference list), titles by the same author are normally listed alphabetically; initial articles (the, a, an) are ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All works by the same person (or same persons in the same order) appear together, regardless of whether they are authored, edited, or translated. For a bibliography of works by a single author, chronological ordering is typical (see section 2 in fig. 14.9). See 14.70.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of author's name (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors' names are normally given as they appear with the source itself (title page or head of article), though certain adjustments may be made to assist identification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First names may be given in full in place of initials; if an author uses a full name in one work and initials in another, use the fuller form consistently. Omit degrees and affiliations. See 14.73 and 15.12.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors who prefer initials
rubrics_metrics.description: For authors who always use initials (e.g., T. S. Eliot), full names should not be supplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions may be made for special cases (e.g., H.D.). Space is added between initials. Cross-references may be appropriate in some cases. See 14.74, 10.12.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name order in notes vs bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: In a note, the author's name is given in normal (text) order; in a bibliography, names are inverted (last name first) for alphabetizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 14.23 and examples throughout 14.75–14.76.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two or three authors: listing and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or three authors (or editors) are listed in the order given in the source; in the bibliography, only the first author's name is inverted and use the conjunction 'and' (not an ampersand).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comma must appear both before and after the first author's given name or initials. Examples and format conventions shown in 14.76–14.78.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works by four to ten authors
rubrics_metrics.description: For works by or edited by four to ten persons, all names are usually given in the bibliography; in notes, include only the first name followed by et al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word order and punctuation are the same as for two or three authors. See examples in 14.77.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works with more than ten authors
rubrics_metrics.description: For works with more than ten authors (common in natural sciences), Chicago recommends listing the first seven authors followed by et al. in the bibliography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where space is limited, alternative policies (e.g., AMA's: list up to six; if more than six list first three then et al.) may be followed. See 14.77.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors with same family name
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more authors (or editors) share the same family name (and are credited as such), repeat the full name in entries even if the family name is not repeated in the source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide full disambiguating forms in both notes and bibliography. See example Kendris & Kendris in 14.78.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's name appearing in title
rubrics_metrics.description: When the author's name appears in the title or subtitle of a cited work (e.g., an autobiography), the note citation may begin with the title, but the bibliography entry should begin with the author's name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though the name is repeated in the title, bibliography ordering should start with the author. See 14.79.

rubrics_metrics.name: No listed author (anonymous works)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author or editor is unknown, the note or bibliography entry should normally begin with the title; an initial article is ignored in alphabetizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using 'Anonymous' unless grouping several anonymous works; if used, 'Anonymous' or 'Anon.' appears at the first entry and 3-em dashes may be used thereafter. If a work is explicitly attributed to 'Anonymous' on the source, cite it as such. See 14.80.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplying guessed or omitted author names in brackets
rubrics_metrics.description: If the authorship is known or guessed at but omitted on the title page, include the name in brackets (with a question mark for uncertainty).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: '[Samuel Horsley], On the Prosodies of the Greek and Latin Languages (London, 1796).' In the bibliography include the bracketed name as part of the entry. See 14.80.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudonyms
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work is attributed to an invented or descriptive name and the author's real name is not known, include '[pseud.]' in brackets after the name; widely used pseudonyms may be treated as real names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the real name is known and of interest, include it in brackets after the pseudonym. If the real name is better known than the pseudonym, use the real name (optionally followed by the pseudonym in brackets). Cross-references may be used between real names and pseudonyms. See 14.81–14.83 and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-references for pseudonyms and alternative names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use cross-references where helpful to point from real names to pseudonyms or vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Format cross-references with 'See' italicized (e.g., 'Carter, Shawn. See Jay-Z.') and consider listing all works under the real name followed by pseudonyms in brackets, or listing under pseudonyms with cross-references from the real name. See 14.82.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative real names and multiple publishing names
rubrics_metrics.description: When a writer has published under different forms of his/her name, list each work under the name that appears with that work unless the difference is merely initials vs full names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references are occasionally useful. See examples in 14.82.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors known by a given name or mononym
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors generally known only by their given names or by a mononym are listed and alphabetized by those names; omit titles like 'King' or 'Saint' unless needed for disambiguation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include alternative or fuller versions of the name only if needed for disambiguation. See examples in 14.83.
